source: Definitions grounded in Congress.gov and Senate.gov glossaries

terms.definition: The Senate's only procedure to end debate and overcome a filibuster; requires 60 votes on most matters.
Extended debate or delay tactics used in the Senate to block or postpone a vote.
The committee meeting where members debate, amend, and rewrite a bill's text before voting to send it to the full chamber.
A committee has voted to send a measure to the full chamber, usually with a written committee report.
The official, final text of a bill exactly as passed by one chamber.
The final version agreed to by both chambers, signed by their presiding officers and sent to the President.
A fast-track House procedure for less-controversial bills: 40 minutes of debate, no floor amendments, and a two-thirds vote to pass.
A STOCK Act disclosure a member must file within 30-45 days of any securities trade over $1,000 — the filings behind this site's stock-conflict signal.
Agreement with no senator objecting — how the Senate conducts most routine business; a single objection blocks it.
The minimum number of members needed to conduct business — a majority of the chamber.
A senator's notice that they will object to a measure or nomination coming to the floor.
A stopgap funding measure that keeps agencies open, usually at current levels, when regular appropriations aren't finished.
A budget procedure letting certain tax and spending bills pass the Senate by simple majority, immune to the filibuster.
A House petition needing 218 signatures to force a bill out of committee and onto the floor.
A temporary House-Senate panel that negotiates one compromise text when the chambers pass different versions.
The wooden box at the House rostrum where representatives drop bills to introduce them.
An unrelated provision attached to a bill that is likely to pass.
One large bill packaging many separate measures into a single vote.
A bill dies if the President neither signs nor vetoes it within 10 days and Congress has adjourned.
Congress enacts a vetoed bill anyway by a two-thirds vote in each chamber.
Legislation with the force of law (also the vehicle for constitutional amendments); a simple or concurrent resolution is not law.
The member who introduces a bill, and the members who formally add their support to it.
A vote where each member's position is recorded by name — the votes shown on this site's bill pages.
The most senior member of a committee's minority party.
The party leader responsible for counting and rounding up votes.
The permanent citation a bill receives when enacted, e.g. P.L. 119-100 — the 100th law of the 119th Congress.
